name: Yaa Asantewaa
info: Yaa Asantewaa, born around 1840 in Besease, was Queen Mother of Ejisu in the Ashanti Empire and led the Asante war against the British in 1900, the War of the Golden Stool; she died in exile in the Seychelles in 1921.

facts.born: around 1840 in Besease, in the Ashanti Empire (now Ghana); daughter of Kwaku Ampoma and Ata Po, and sister of Afrane Panin, who became chief of Edweso
facts.died: 17 October 1921, in exile in the Seychelles
facts.role: Queen Mother of Ejisu, appointed by her brother, the Ejisuhene; regent of the Ejisu–Juaben district from 1896; war leader of the Asante in the War of the Golden Stool, 1900
facts.known: her appointment as Queen Mother of Ejisu; her speech to the Asante council against the British demand for the Golden Stool; command of the Asante forces in the War of the Golden Stool; the siege of the British fort at Kumasi; exile to the Seychelles

t: Born around 1840 into a farming family at Besease, Yaa Asantewaa became Queen Mother of Ejisu through her brother, the Ejisuhene, an office that carried responsibility for the Golden Stool and a voice in choosing the next king.

When the British exiled King Prempeh I in 1896 and their governor demanded the Golden Stool, she urged the remaining Asante leaders to fight, and in 1900 she was chosen war leader, the first and only woman given that role in Asante history.

The rebellion of 1900 besieged the British fort at Kumasi and ended in defeat and her exile to the Seychelles, where she died in 1921; the Stool itself was never handed over, and she is remembered in Ghana as a figure of resistance to colonial rule.
dyk: In the council that debated what to do about the governor's demand for the Golden Stool, Yaa Asantewaa is said to have told the chiefs to exchange their loincloths for her undergarments if they would not fight, and then to have seized a gun and fired a shot in front of the men.
ev: Yaa Asantewaa is born in Besease, daughter of Kwaku Ampoma and Ata Po
A civil war begins in the Ashanti Confederacy and lasts until 1888
Her brother dies, and as Queen Mother she nominates her own grandson as Ejisuhene
The British exile her grandson, King Prempeh I and other Asante leaders to the Seychelles; she becomes regent of the Ejisu–Juaben district
The Asante lay siege to the British fort at Kumasi; she is chosen war leader of the Asante forces
The British annex the territory of the Asante Empire and make the Asante a protectorate
She dies in exile in the Seychelles
Prempeh I and the other exiles are allowed to return to Asante, and her remains are returned for a royal burial

sections.early:
Yaa Asantewaa was born around 1840 in Besease, the daughter of Kwaku Ampoma and Ata Po. Her brother Afrane Panin became the chief of Edweso, a nearby community. Her childhood passed without incident, and she grew up to cultivate crops on the land around Boankra. She entered a polygamous marriage with a man from Kumasi and had a daughter. She was a successful farmer and mother.

She belonged to a society organised on matrilineal lines, in which lineage is traced through women descended from a common female ancestor. The Ashanti held that a person's blood comes from the mother and spirit from the father. Among the Akan, the hierarchy of male stools was complemented by female counterparts. The head of a division, the ohene, and the head of an autonomous political community, the Amanhene, each had a female counterpart, the ohemaa, who sat on their councils. The ohemaa and the ohene shared the same mogya, or localised matrilineage. In a village, the heads of the matrilineages formed the village council, and for each village an obaa panyin looked after the affairs of its women and sat on that council. Women who held stools took part in judicial and legislative business, in the making and unmaking of war, and in the distribution of land.
sections.rise:
Her older brother, Nana Akwasi Afrane Okpase, held a powerful position in the empire and selected her as Queen Mother of Ejisu. The post was a prestigious one. The Queen Mother was responsible for protecting the Golden Stool, advising the King of Ashanti and choosing candidates for the next king. The queen mother was the sister of the chief and head of kinship relations.

During her brother's time in office, she saw the Ashanti Confederacy pass through events that threatened its future, among them a civil war from 1883 to 1888. Her brother died in 1894, and she used her right as Queen Mother to nominate her own grandson as Ejisuhene. In 1896 the British exiled this grandson to the Seychelles, along with the King of Asante, Prempeh I, and other members of the Asante government. Yaa Asantewaa then became regent of the Ejisu–Juaben district. After Prempeh's exile, the British governor of the Gold Coast, Frederick Hodgson, demanded the Golden Stool, the symbol of the Asante nation. The demand led the remaining members of the Asante government to meet secretly at Kumasi to discuss how to secure their king's return.
sections.deeds:
The members of the council disagreed on how to proceed. Yaa Asantewaa, who was present, rose and addressed them. She asked how a proud and brave people could sit back while white men took away their king and chiefs and humiliated them with a demand for the Golden Stool, which she said meant only money to the white men. She said she would not pay one predwan to the governor, and that if the chiefs of Asante behaved like cowards and would not fight, they should exchange their loincloths for her undergarments. To show her determination she seized a gun and fired a shot in front of the men.

A number of regional Asante kings chose her as war leader of the Asante fighting force, the first and only time in Asante history that a woman was given that role. A longer speech is also attributed to her, in which she recalled that the British had occupied the land and declared Ashanti a protectorate, had burnt the palace in the reign of King Karikari, and had arrested and deported the king, and she called on the men to defend the Golden Stool. She challenged gender roles and urged women to stand up to fight. The war, called the War of the Golden Stool or the Yaa Asantewaa War, was fought with an army of 5,000 under her leadership. From March 1900 the rebels laid siege to the British fort at Kumasi, where the British had sought refuge.
sections.opponents:
Her chief opponents were the British colonial authorities. The Gold Coast governor, Frederick Hodgson, demanded the Golden Stool, which had been a revered symbol of the Ashanti nation's soul since the 17th century. After several months of siege, the governor sent a force of 1,400 to put down the rebellion. More than 2,000 Ashanti warriors lost their lives in the fighting, and approximately 1,000 British troops were also killed. This was the highest death toll of the Anglo-Asante wars. The fighting lasted six months. Yaa Asantewaa and a group of her advisers were captured and sent into exile in the Seychelles.

There was disagreement on the Asante side as well. When the remaining leaders met at Kumasi to decide how to win back their king, they disagreed on the course to take, and her speech was aimed at those who hesitated. She questioned the male leaders' response to British colonisation. Despite the British victory, the Golden Stool was never turned over: a false one was delivered to the governor and the real Stool was kept hidden.
sections.last:
The rebellion was the last of the Anglo-Asante wars, a series that ran through the 19th century. On 1 January 1902 the British annexed the territory that the Asante Empire had controlled for almost a century, and the Asante became a protectorate of the British crown. Yaa Asantewaa and her advisers had by then been sent into exile in the Seychelles. Fifteen of her closest advisers went with her.

She died in exile in the Seychelles on 17 October 1921. Three years after her death, on 17 December 1924, King Prempeh I and the other remaining members of the exiled Asante court were allowed to return to Asante. Prempeh made sure that the remains of Yaa Asantewaa and the other exiled Ashantis were returned for a proper royal burial. In 1920 a group of African railroad builders found the hidden Golden Stool and vandalised it. The Ashanti people sentenced them to death, but the British authorities exiled them from the Gold Coast colony before they were killed.
sections.legacy:
The Asante protectorate gained independence as part of Ghana on 6 March 1957, which is presented as the realisation of her dream of an Asante free of colonial rule. The Golden Stool is still used to initiate and crown the Asantehene. She remains a known figure in Ashanti history and in the broader history of Ghana for her part in confronting British colonialism, and Ghanaians today see her as a queen mother who exercised her political and social right to defend her kingdom. A song remembers her as the woman who fights before cannons.

The Yaa Asantewaa Girls' Secondary School was established in Kumasi in 1960. In 2000, the hundredth anniversary of the war, Ghana held a week-long celebration with a festival, an international conference, a women's convention and a funeral service for her remains; a museum was dedicated to her at Kwaso in the Ejisu–Juaben District on 3 August 2000. A fire on 23 July 2004 destroyed several items there, among them her sandals and battle dress. The current queen mother of Ejisu is Yaa Asantewaa II. The Yaa Asantewaa Centre, an African–Caribbean arts and community centre, was established in Maida Vale, west London, in 1986 and named after her.

summary: Yaa Asantewaa (c. 1840–1921) was Queen Mother of Ejisu in the Ashanti Empire. After the British exiled King Prempeh I and demanded the Golden Stool, she was chosen war leader of the Asante in 1900. The war ended in defeat and her exile to the Seychelles, where she died.
notes: The article is short and its Biography section gives little of her early life; the 'early' section leans on the article's section on the social roles of Asante women, stated as the setting rather than as facts about her own household.

Her brother's name varies: Nana Akwasi Afrane Okese in the lede, Nana Akwasi Afrane Okpase in the body, and Afrane Panin as chief of Edweso. The article may be speaking of one man or two; the 'rise' section names him only by the first two forms and facts.born uses Afrane Panin as the article's own phrase for the chief of Edweso. Editor to read.
The list of fifteen advisers exiled with her includes Nana Akwasi Afrane Okpase, her brother, who the article says died in 1894; the list was left out. It also includes Nana Osei Tutu II.
The article says she was appointed Queen Mother by her brother, yet also that the queen mother was the chief's sister, so the post is described consistently as her brother's appointment.

Exile: the article says her grandson and Prempeh I were exiled in 1896; it says she was exiled to the Seychelles after the 1900 fighting, with no year given for the sailing. The 'ev' list has no event for it.

Death toll: the article gives more than 2,000 Ashanti and approximately 1,000 British killed, and calls it the highest toll of the Anglo-Asante wars; the figures are not attributed to any estimator. The siege 'lasted 6 months' while the rebellion began 'March 1900'.

The first speech is given in the article with a Twi phrase; the second, longer speech is placed by the article in her words but its wording looks modern and its source is not named, so it is described as 'attributed to her'. Editor to decide whether to keep it.
The Golden Stool: the article says it is 18 inches tall and 12 inches wide and was 'never turned over'; this was left out as detail. The 1920 episode of railway builders is given as in the article.
The article says the stool 'is never to be sat on'; not used.

Left out as not about her life or as the article's own reflection: tourism figures, the television documentary, the stage show, the radio drama, the Sons of Kemet track, the German award and the 2024 British Museum painting.
The article says she was 'an intellectual, a politician, a human rights activist, a queen and a war leader'; left out as an unattributed assessment.
Sections 'opponents' and 'last' are under the 1,100-character minimum or near it because the article gives little on critics; no critic of her is named in the article.
References: left empty for the editor; the article's bibliography lists Boahen and Boahen (2004), Harvey (2020), Day (2004) and Agyeman-Duah (1999) among its sources.
